youtube.baslik: Assessing Children with Multiple Disabilities | Lesson 171 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How do we assess children who have other disabilities besides hearing loss? In this lesson we cover how behavioral tests are adapted for autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy and vision loss, the role of objective tests, and family-centered teamwork.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Madell, Flexer, Wolfe and Schafer, Pediatric Audiology: Diagnosis, Technology, and Management; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Joint Committee on Infant Hearing, Year 2019 Position Statement; Gallaudet Research Institute, Annual Survey of Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children and Youth.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how to adapt audiological assessment for children who have other disabilities besides hearing loss.
We will cover test adaptations for autism, cerebral palsy and vision loss, the role of objective tests, and teamwork.

sahneler.baslik: Why do we see it *so often*?
cumleler: Multiple disabilities means that a child has more than one disability at the same time.
In a large US survey of deaf and hard of hearing students, about forty percent were reported to have an additional disability.
One reason is shared risk factors.
Prematurity, congenital infections, lack of oxygen at birth and syndromes can affect both hearing and development.
CHARGE syndrome, which we saw in the genetics lessons, was an example where hearing and vision can be affected together.
An additional disability can delay recognition of hearing loss; a child's lack of response to sound may be blamed on the other diagnosis.
Conversely, hearing loss can also lead to a developmental problem being recognized later.
Assessment starts before the visit: learn the child's strengths, communication style and sensitivities from the family and care team.
The test method is chosen by developmental level, not chronological age, as we saw at the start of the pediatric lessons.
Then consider how the child can respond to sound: turning the head, shifting the eyes, touching a switch, or play.
The behavioral method is adapted to the child; insisting on the standard method often gives unreliable results.
Objective tests such as tympanometry, otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response are always in the battery for these children.
All results are tested against each other using the cross-check principle; no decision rests on a single test.

maddeler.metin: New places and touch are hard
Hearing loss may also be present

cumleler: Autism spectrum disorder is a condition with difficulties in social communication and repetitive behaviors.
These children may not respond to their name or to speech, so families often suspect hearing loss first.
So measuring hearing reliably is an important step in an autism assessment.
Some children are oversensitive to certain sounds; they cover their ears and avoid sounds such as a vacuum cleaner or hand dryer.
A new environment, wearing earphones or having the ear touched may be met with anxiety and protest.
Hearing loss can also occur in autistic children, so hearing should be measured before lack of response is put down to autism.
Conversely, if social communication differences persist in a child with hearing loss, assessment for autism should not be delayed.
A simple visual schedule that shows the test steps in pictures lets the child know in advance what will happen.
Earphones or insert tips can be introduced at home through play before the visit; this is called desensitization.
Waiting time is kept short, and a calm room with little light and noise is chosen.
A favorite toy and a familiar adult nearby clearly improve cooperation.
If needed, the assessment is split into several short sessions, collecting the most important information first each time.
If behavioral testing is not possible, thresholds are estimated with objective tests; this is better than forcing the child.

maddeler.metin: Motor limits change the response mode

cumleler: Cerebral palsy describes lasting disorders of movement and posture caused by damage to the developing brain.
Even if a child hears a sound, turning the head or pressing a button may be hard; no response must not be mistaken for no hearing.
First, make sure the child sits comfortably and steadily; their own wheelchair or a parent's lap may be the best option.
The response mode is chosen by what the child can do: shifting the eyes to the sound, touching a large switch, or making a sound.
Talking with the family and the child's physical therapist beforehand helps a lot in recognizing these responses.
Severe newborn jaundice and lack of oxygen are risk factors for cerebral palsy and for auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, or ANSD.
So in these children, otoacoustic emissions, or OAEs, and the auditory brainstem response, or ABR, are assessed together.
Constant muscle tension or involuntary movements can create artifacts in the ABR recording.
So recording is often done during sleep or under sedation; the decision on sedation belongs to the physician.
We can adapt the visual reinforcement audiometry setup for a child with motor limitations.
The reinforcer toy is placed at an angle the child can see without turning the head much.
In a child who cannot turn the head, an experienced observer watches for an eye gaze response.
If the child responds slowly, the response window is lengthened; a hurried assessment misses responses.
Control trials with no sound are also run to weed out false responses.
These adaptations keep the logic of the standard method; they only fit the form of the response to the child.

maddeler.metin: Loss in two senses: early intervention

cumleler: Visual reinforcement audiometry, as the name says, depends on the child seeing the reinforcer.
In a child whose vision is severely affected, this method cannot be used as it is.
For a child with low vision, bright, high-contrast lighted reinforcers can be placed in the best part of the visual field.
For a blind child, a vibrating toy, touch or favorite music can be used as reinforcement.
In play audiometry, objects that can be found by touch, such as rings or blocks, are chosen.
Children with combined vision and hearing loss need early, specialized support for communication and mobility skills.
Retinopathy of prematurity and CHARGE and Usher syndromes are examples of conditions that can affect both senses.
A blind child cannot see what is happening in the room, so each step is explained in words first.
Before earphones, a probe or a bone vibrator go near the ear, they are placed in the child's hand to explore by touch.
Sudden touches can startle the child; calling the child by name before touching is a good habit.
Having the family nearby gives security and helps the child work out where sounds come from.
Giving the child time to explore new objects improves cooperation for the rest of the test.
Tympanometry shows middle ear status; middle ear fluid is also common in these children.
Otoacoustic emissions show outer hair cell function quickly, with no response needed from the child.
The acoustic reflex gives information about the integrity of the reflex arc formed by the auditory pathway and the facial nerve.
The auditory brainstem response and the auditory steady-state response, or ASSR, give ear- and frequency-specific threshold estimates.
These tests need long, quiet recordings and may require sedation; that decision belongs to the physician.
The audiologist prepares the test plan in advance to make the best use of sedation time.
Objective results are confirmed with behavioral tests as the child's development allows.
The family is at the center of these children's assessment; they know the child best and see the child every day.
Pediatricians, pediatric neurologists, eye doctors and ENT physicians carry out the medical evaluation.
The speech-language therapist assesses the child's communication style and how the child uses auditory input.
The special education teacher helps plan classroom adaptations and assistive tools such as remote microphones.
Physical and occupational therapists offer important advice on correct positioning and device use during testing.
In this team, the audiologist provides the hearing data and lays the auditory basis for device decisions.

sahneler.metin: Before the visit, ask the family three questions: what does the child like, what upsets the child, and how does the child react to sound?
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: have a short phone call with the family a few days before the appointment.
Ask what the child likes, what upsets the child, and how the child reacts to sounds at home.
These three answers let you choose the reinforcer, set up the room and decide the test order.
State the adaptations you used clearly in your report; repeating the same conditions next time makes comparison easier.

maddeler.metin: Objective tests always in the battery

cumleler: Many children with hearing loss have an additional disability; shared risk factors and diagnoses masking each other matter.
The behavioral method is chosen by developmental level, not age; the response mode and reinforcer are adapted to the child.
Tympanometry, OAEs, the acoustic reflex and ABR support behavioral results through the cross-check principle.
The assessment is planned with the family and the child's care team, and the adaptations are written in the report.

sahneler.soru: What changes in visual reinforcement for a blind child?
sahneler.aciklama: Reinforcement is given by _touch_ or sound.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: for a child with severely affected vision, which part of visual reinforcement audiometry should be adapted?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the type of reinforcer.
The child cannot see a lighted toy, so vibration, touch or a favorite sound is used as reinforcement.
